Correct answer: \(-4\)
Rule. The whole interval equals the sum of its pieces. Subtract the known piece to get the missing one.
\(\displaystyle \int_{a}^{c}f=\int_{a}^{b}f+\int_{b}^{c}f\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\int_{b}^{c}f=\int_{a}^{c}f-\int_{a}^{b}f\)
Original integral. We want
\(\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{4}f(x)\,dx\)
Apply the rule.
\(\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{4}f(x)\,dx=\int_{-5}^{4}f(x)\,dx-\int_{-5}^{-1}f(x)\,dx\)
Substitute the numbers.
\(\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{4}f(x)\,dx=7-11\)
Algebra.
\(\displaystyle \int_{-1}^{4}f(x)\,dx=-4\)
Why it works. Removing the piece from \(-5\) to \(-1\) from the whole leaves only the piece from \(-1\) to \(4\).
Answer. \(-4\)

Part 2 is correct.
Divide \([0,1]\) into \(n\) equal subintervals. Each one has width
\(\displaystyle \Delta x=\frac{b-a}{n}=\frac{1-0}{n}=\frac{1}{n}\)
The right endpoint of the \(k\)th subinterval is
\(\displaystyle x_k=a+k\,\Delta x=0+k\cdot\frac{1}{n}=\frac{k}{n}\)
The definite integral is the limit of the right-endpoint sums.
\(\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}\left(-x^{2}\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n}f(x_k)\,\Delta x\)
Replace \(x_k\) and \(\Delta x\) with the expressions we just found.
\(\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}\left(-x^{2}\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left[-\left(\frac{k}{n}\right)^{2}\right]\frac{1}{n}\)
Multiply out the summand and write it as separate terms.
\(\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}\left(-x^{2}\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(-\frac{k^{2}}{n^{3}}\right)\)
Pull each constant outside the sum. Then use this summation formula.
\(\displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{2}=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\)
This is the sum of the first n squares.
Substitute it into the sum.
\(\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}\left(-x^{2}\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[-\frac{1}{n^{3}}\cdot \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}\right]\)
Simplify the algebra so the expression involves only \(n\).
\(\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}\left(-x^{2}\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[-\frac{1}{6}\cdot \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{n^{2}}\right]\)
To see what happens as \(n\) grows, split each fraction into separate terms.
\(\displaystyle \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{n^{2}}=2+\frac{3}{n}+\frac{1}{n^{2}}\)
\(\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}\left(-x^{2}\right)\,dx=\lim_{n\to\infty}\left[-\frac{1}{6}\cdot \left(2+\frac{3}{n}+\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right)\right]\)
Now take the limit. As \(n\to\infty\), \(\frac{1}{n}\to 0\) and \(\frac{1}{n^{2}}\to 0\), so every term with \(n\) in the denominator vanishes.
\(\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}\left(-x^{2}\right)\,dx=-\frac{1}{6}\cdot \left(2+0+0\right)\)
Simplify.
\(\displaystyle \int_{0}^{1}\left(-x^{2}\right)\,dx=-\frac{1}{3}\)
